Artisan, the AI sales agent startup founded by Jaspar Carmichael-Jack, recently raised $25 million in Series A funding, led by Glade Brook Capital, with participation from Y Combinator, Day One Ventures, HubSpot Ventures, and others. Founded in 2024, Artisan initially garnered attention with its bold “Stop Hiring Humans” campaign, positioning itself in the rapidly growing AI sales development representative (SDR) market. Despite early-stage challenges, including customer churn and issues with AI performance, the company has made significant strides, refining its AI agent, Ava, and achieving $5 million in annual recurring revenue with 250 customers. Artisan is also working on new AI products, such as Aaron for inbound messaging and Aria, a meeting manager assistant, both set to launch by the end of 2025. Carmichael-Jack, who co-founded the company with Sam Stallings, continues to steer Artisan as CEO, emphasizing the importance of human labor in AI-driven environments.\

Overheard at the Mercury Bookstore:

Luca Pacioli: Ancient Double-Entry Bookkeeping, published by Mercury. @mercuryfi \
\
A contemporary republication of John B. Geijsbeek’s 1914 English translation of Luca Pacioli’s landmark 1494 treatise on bookkeeping. Redesigned and newly typeset at the exact dimensions of the original 1914 edition, the book brings the translation together with original pages, diagrams and historical material in a new editorial structure.\
\
Pacioli’s text was the first printed description of double-entry bookkeeping, codifying the system of debits, credits, journals and ledgers that became foundational to modern accounting. The subject has particular relevance for Mercury, whose financial tools for businesses are built on many of these same underlying principles.\
\
The section-sewn hardcover features an exposed spine, silver foil typography and a violet-painted top edge, and is housed in a flexographically printed box.\
\
Published by @mercuryfi \
Edited by Sarah Robinson\
Design by @studiolin\
Printed and bound by Ofset Yapimevi, Istanbul

Bears Ears National Monument in Utah was the first national monument in the United States created at the urging of Tribal Nations, and the first where a coalition of Tribal Nations collaborated with federal agencies to craft a management plan for a national monument. But long before it was a monument, it was home, and it remains a living homeland today.\
 \
Hopi, Zuni, Diné, Ute, and other Indigenous peoples have lived in and cared for these lands since time immemorial. And the five Tribal Nations that came together to lead the modern effort to protect Bears Ears—the Hopi Tribe, Navajo Nation, Ute Mountain Ute Tribe, Pueblo of Zuni and Ute Indian Tribe—have worked to safeguard these sacred places for their communities and future generations, while helping ensure people can continue to climb, trail run and recreate respectfully.\
 \
It's our responsibility to stand with Tribal leaders against the illegal proclamation to shrink Bears Ears by roughly 91%, exposing thousands of culturally significant sites, traditional plants and medicines, and an ecologically critical landscape to extractive industries.\

In a ​2008 paper​ published in the Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, researchers at the University of Virginia sought to study the impact of social support on how we perceive challenges.\
\
In the first study, the researchers had a group of participants stand at the base of a steep 26° hill wearing a heavy backpack. Some of the participants were alone, while others were paired with a friend. Then they asked the participants to estimate the hill’s steepness.\
\
The findings were fascinating:\
\
Participants who were paired with a friend estimated the hill to be significantly less steep than those who were alone.\
\
Relationship duration with the friend correlated negatively with perceived steepness. The longer the friendship, the gentler the hill appeared.\
\
In a follow-up study, the researchers had the participants stand alone and simply imagine either a supportive person (friend), neutral person (store clerk), or negative person (someone who had betrayed them).\
\
Once again, the results were clear:\
\
Participants who imagined a supportive person saw the hill as less steep than those who imagined neutral or negative people.\
\
The closeness and warmth of the imagined relationship were negatively correlated with perceived steepness. The better the relationship, the gentler the hill appeared.\
\
The researchers concluded that the brain treats supportive relationships as a psychological energy resource. When you feel connected, your brain effectively lightens the load.\
\
The challenge doesn’t change, but the perception of that challenge does.\
\
Because challenges and struggles are inevitable.\
\
But facing them alone is optional.\

Istanbul is famous for its outsized cat population who you’ll find roaming free, keeping watch, and mingling with the humans. Meet the cats who rule the city.\
\
By breakfast, the cats are already making the rounds. In Istanbul, they turn up in cafés, markets, bookstores, waterfronts and anywhere people gather.\
\
Istanbul’s official visitor guide gives cats top billing and calls them the “Royalty of Istanbul.”\
\
Istanbul’s cats are independent by design. Most don’t belong to one person, and they’re perfectly happy picking their own lookout points, routes and favorite corners.\
\
Istanbul is often cited as home to one of the largest concentrated street-cat populations in the world.\
\
If there’s a spot to claim, a cat has probably claimed it first. What’s ours is theirs.\
\
Istanbul’s cats are professional photobombers. They show up in wedding photos, tourist’s shots, and plenty of camera rolls they weren’t invited into.\
\
Istanbul helps take care of its street cats with veterinary care, vaccinations and dedicated “paw parks” where animals have space to play. Resist the urge to scoop one up and take it with you. Some have entire neighborhoods looking after them.\
\
An entire film was made about the cats of Istanbul. According to the director, “The real soul of the city is actually, I think, the cats.”\
\
Why are they so comfortable here? Because they’ve been here for centuries. They arrived on trading ships as far back as Byzantium, originally brought in to control pesky critters in cargo holds.
Ferries, trams, cats, the sea, and then the call to prayer rising over it all, and for a moment everything pauses. This is your sign to visit Istanbul.

The two continents of Istanbul meet at the water, where the city is always in motion between Europe and Asia. Follow the ferries between antique shops, family recipes, and the perfect afternoon coffee. Make your way to the best of Istanbul with a few tips from the people who know it best.\
\
For more than 20 years, Özge has lived in Istanbul cooking recipes passed down through generations. Her view of the city starts at her neighborhood market and stretches well beyond the kitchen, to antique shops, döner counters, and cafés across Europe and Asia.\
\
Çukurcuma is one of Beyoğlu’s best-known areas for antiques, with dealers, galleries and cafés lining the side streets. It’s one of the European side’s go-to neighborhoods for browsing.\
\
A La Turca is a four-story home turned antique shop. It grew out of a collectors personal collection, which is why the shop feels more curated than conventional.\
\
A La Turca house\
\
The best büfe-style döner is tucked just behind the Grand Bazaar. Kasım works the spit at Dönerci Hacı Osman’ın Yeri, where there’s a daily line until the food runs out. He keeps it moving and may even hand you a taste while you wait.\
\
The seasoned lamb is the star, piled with whole sweet peppers, freshly cut tomatoes and pickles. Get it on a plate, in pita or in their soft bread; there’s only one meat to choose from, so all you have to decide is the size.\
\
The Galata Bridge crosses the Golden Horn between the Old City and Beyoğlu. Walk across with the fishermen lining the rails while ferries pass underneath, and you get one of the best views of the Old City.\
\
From the European side, the ferry crosses the Bosphorus to Kadıköy in Asia. Grab a seat outside and watch Istanbul on both sides of the water.\
\
In Kadıköy, head to Yeldeğirmeni for street art and independent cafés. Slow down and soak it all in at Ikarus Coffee House, known for serious coffee and easy living-room vibe. \
\
📍Rasimpaşa Mah., Yeldeğirmeni Sk. No:11\/A\
\
Order the iced oat flat white, made with espresso and oat milk over ice. The café also hosts live music, so check their feed before you go to see what’s on.\

Lasagne meets soup. Ultimate comfort food - you’re welcome 🍝 Recipe below ⬇️ \
\
12 Tesco 3 Ingredient Meatballs\
2 tbsp olive oil\
1 large onion, finely chopped\
1 carrot, peeled and finely chopped\
6 garlic cloves, finely minced\
2 tbsp red pesto\
½  tsp red chilli flakes\
1 tbsp dried oregano\
500g Tesco Italian passata with garlic & herbs\
1 chicken stock cube made up with 1.3L water \
200g dried lasagne sheets, broken into shards\
75g whipping cream\
100g ricotta\
30g Parmesan, grated\
½ bunch fresh basil, roughly torn\
\
1. Heat 2 tbsp of the olive oil in a large pot over a medium heat. Add the meatballs and cook for 8-10 minutes , browning on each side or until golden brown all over.\
\
2. Remove the meatballs from the pan. Sauté the onion and carrot for 10 minutes or until softened.\
\
3. Add the garlic and cook until fragrant. Follow with the passata, pesto, chilli flakes, oregano and stock. Stir through the whipping cream and bring to a simmer. Cook for 15 minutes and season with salt and pepper.\
\
4. Add the broken lasagne sheets and return the meatballs to the pan. Cook for 10 minutes or until the pasta is al dente, stirring often. Add a splash of water if needed to loosen the soup.\
\
5. Serve into individual bowls and top with a dollop of ricotta, grated Parmesan and fresh basil.

The best way to make university useful for your career isn’t always getting perfect grades.\
\
First, work out how much your grades actually matter. If a first-class degree or 4.0 GPA will meaningfully improve your career prospects, then obviously it’s worth optimising for them.\
\
But for many careers, employers stop caring about your grades fairly quickly.\
\
So, use some of your spare time to go on side quests and build valuable skills. Learn to code, edit videos, design websites, write, sell or use AI tools.\
\
Your degree might help you get your first job, but the skills you build alongside it could shape the rest of your career. \
\
And if you want to know what skills you have that could become a business idea, comment CRAFT and I’ll send you my custom GPT that will interview you and help figure out what your craft skills are 👇
Advice to my younger self 😌

When I was 18, I got scammed out of £1,000.\
\
At the time, that was literally all the money I had. I’d spent two years tutoring maths for £15 an hour to save for a MacBook Air, only to discover I’d paid £1,000 for an old laptop worth about £200.\
\
It was painful. But I decided I was going to make the money back, and then make 10 times more.\
\
That decision prompted me to start my first proper business.\
\
Over the next few years, it generated more than £1 million in revenue. I eventually sold it and used the money to start another business, which has since generated over £10 million.\
\
Obviously, I wouldn’t recommend getting scammed.\
\
But sometimes the worst moments can become surprisingly useful fuel for whatever you do next.\
\
And if that next step for you is taking the leap to start and build your own business to $100k a year, comment FOUNDATIONS and I’ll send you my free 7-lesson course.

Comment FOUNDATIONS if you want to build your own $100k a year lifestyle business - to get access to my free 7-lesson course from @lifestylebusinessacademy 👇\
\
I used to assume that a successful business should keep growing: more revenue, more people, more complexity.\
\
But there’s a difficult middle ground between a small lifestyle business and a larger performance business.\
\
Once the team grows beyond roughly 12 people, you often need proper management layers and a completely different way of operating.\
\
Every time we’ve reached 15–18 people, things have started to break, and we’ve ended up returning to a smaller core team.\
\
Right now, that’s what I want.\
\
I’ve got a kid, we’ve recently moved to Hong Kong, and I want more space for family, health and life outside work.\
\
Maybe one day I’ll want to build a huge company. But for now, I’m choosing fun, freedom and flexibility.\
\
Because bigger isn’t automatically better. It depends on the life you’re trying to build.

If I were starting a business today with no audience, I’d keep it simple.\
\
I’d choose a skill I already have like content creation, marketing or AI automation and offer it as a service to someone in my existing network.\
\
At first, I’d charge a discounted rate and offer a strong guarantee. The goal wouldn’t be to maximise profit.\
\
It would be to get a great result, testimonial and case study.\
\
Then I’d use that proof to find more clients.\
\
Over time, I’d hire someone, productise the service and potentially turn it into a product. Alongside that, I’d build a personal brand around the skill.\
\
You don’t need an audience or a perfectly scalable idea to begin, so don’t let that hold you back.\
\
Start by solving one real problem for one real person and build from there.\
\
Comment FOUNDATIONS for my free 7-lesson course on how to build your $100k a year business with a full-time job.

Comment FOUNDATIONS for my free 7-lesson course on how to build a $100k a year business if I were starting again with a full-time job 👇\
\
I made my first £30 online when I was 12.\
\
I’d decided to learn website design, so I emailed everyone I knew asking if they needed a website. One person said yes, and only then did I figure out the HTML and CSS. \
\
I had no degree, no experience and, frankly, very little idea what I was doing. I just found someone with a problem, offered to solve it and learned the skills along the way.\
\
That £30 completely changed how I thought about work. I realised I could get paid to learn something I’d happily have done for free.\
\
And honestly, that’s still some of my favourite advice for new entrepreneurs: don’t wait until you feel qualified. Find a real problem, offer to solve it, and work out the details as you go.
